section: What this section does and does not establish (under 'The worst case in the literature: epinephrine with no anesthetic')
sentence_as_it_stands: It does not show that oxygen holds up in *skin*: the one study that measured skin oxygen for hours found it halved and slow to recover, and although that study injected epinephrine with no anesthetic in a rat, nobody has done the equivalent measurement in a human wheal.
quote: The local tissue-oxygen tension in the skin was studied, when adrenaline, noradrenaline and Octapressinm Sandoz were used as vasoconstrictors in local anaesthetic agents injected subcutaneously on the forearms of healthy human subjects. … We made measurements 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after the injection of the anaesthetic.
corrected_wording: It does not show that oxygen holds up in skin: the rat study that followed skin oxygen for eight hours found it halved and slow to recover. One human measurement over hours exists and it is much older and much smaller: Klingenstrom and Westermark 1964 (PMID 14272296) measured local tissue-oxygen tension in the forearm skin of nine healthy subjects at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after subcutaneous lidocaine with adrenaline or with noradrenaline, against a felypressin-containing site on the same arm, and found the catecholamine sites lower, with a median of 87 per cent of the felypressin site for adrenaline. Nobody has made the equivalent measurement at a human wheal.
notes: Same sentence as claim C084, which this paper's own question was asked for; recorded here because it gives the page location and because the correction is larger than the claim update alone shows. The paper's human measurement is not a like-for-like replacement for Miller's: the route was subcutaneous rather than intradermal, the adrenaline strength was stronger than the page's, there was no pre-injection baseline and no plain-anaesthetic site, the readings are only percentages of the felypressin site rather than absolute tensions, and n was nine with incomplete data in three. Its direction is also milder than Miller's rat result rather than more alarming. The two quoted parts are from PDF pages 5 and 2 of the paper. Page fetch showed no truncation flags; verification state on the page is 'unverified'.

section: What counts as strong evidence for your question (the ranked tiers)
sentence_as_it_stands: Next: animal, intact skin. Adds hours of recording and adds tissue oxygen, at the cost of the species difference.
quote: The oxygen tension was-measured in the infiltrated zone, at the same depth as the injections. … We made measurements 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after the injection of the anaesthetic.
corrected_wording: The ranking places hours of recording and tissue oxygen in the animal tier. One human study in the tier above it has both: Klingenstrom and Westermark 1964 (PMID 14272296) measured local tissue-oxygen tension in intact human forearm skin at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours after injection, at a stronger adrenaline strength than this document's, and the tier line 'almost all stop measuring at ten minutes' therefore has an exception that reports tissue oxygen rather than flow.
notes: Recorded as low because the sentence is accurate on its most natural reading - as a description of this document's own source set, hours of recording plus tissue oxygen do come only from the animal tier, and the human tier above it is hedged as 'almost all stop measuring at ten minutes'. It is recorded at all because as a statement about the literature it has an exception: Klingenstrom and Westermark 1964 is human, intact skin, measured over hours, and the measurement is tissue oxygen. Weighting it again should take account of what that study gives up: a relative rather than absolute oxygen measure, no baseline, a subcutaneous rather than intradermal route, a stronger adrenaline strength and nine subjects.

section: What can actually be bought in Mexico? > Felypressin is a vasoconstrictor under a different name; and the Sources entry for Olgart 1977
sentence_as_it_stands: It is not adrenaline and it does not behave like adrenaline in tissue.
quote: The local tissue-oxygen tension in the skin was studied, when adrenaline, noradrenaline and Octapressinm Sandoz were used as vasoconstrictors in local anaesthetic agents injected subcutaneously on the forearms of healthy human subjects.
corrected_wording: It is not adrenaline and it does not behave like adrenaline in tissue. Every local comparison cited here is in dental pulp (cats, rabbits), a tissue the page itself notes is unlike skin, but the comparison has also been made in human skin: Klingenstrom and Westermark 1964 (PMID 14272296) injected lidocaine with adrenaline, with noradrenaline and with felypressin at three sites on the forearms of nine healthy subjects and measured local tissue-oxygen tension at 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 hours, finding it lower at the catecholamine sites (adrenaline median 87 per cent of the felypressin site) and equal to uninjected skin at the felypressin site.
notes: Recorded as low because the sentence is accurate: felypressin does behave differently from adrenaline in tissue, and the 1964 study agrees with it. It is recorded because every local comparison the page cites is dental pulp (Olgart 1977 cats, Tachibana 2021 rabbits) or myocardium (Inagawa 2010 rabbits), and the page's own source entry names the limit - 'Limits: cats, dental pulp, a tissue enclosed in rigid bone and unlike skin' - while a human skin comparison of the same two vasoconstrictors exists and is not cited anywhere on the page (a text search of the fetched page for 'Klingen' returned nothing). It is small: nine subjects, subcutaneous rather than intradermal, no baseline, and only percentages of the felypressin site. No truncation flags on the fetch.

section: What can actually be bought in Mexico? > That does not make it harmless, and it does not make it acceptable here
sentence_as_it_stands: And whatever its potency relative to adrenaline, it is in the cartridge for the same purpose: to narrow the vessels around the injection so the drug leaves more slowly. Rejecting vasoconstriction rejects this too, on the same grounds — and the observation that drove that rejection, blanching outlasting the analgesia, argues for more suspicion of a longer-acting peptide, not less.
quote: Following the administration of Octapressin, the pallor persisted unchanged for 3.5 hours or longer, and no cyanosis appeared.
corrected_wording: The inference that a longer-acting peptide deserves more suspicion on blanching has a direct human skin measurement behind it: in Klingenstrom and Westermark 1964 (PMID 14272296) the pallor at the felypressin site in human forearm skin persisted unchanged for 3.5 hours or longer, which was the whole observation period, while the adrenaline and noradrenaline sites turned cyanotic centrally within the first hour and kept only a narrow pale rim.
notes: Recorded as low because the sentence is accurate on its natural reading - it is offered as an argument, not as a sourced finding, and the page's 'What has no source' section does not list it. It is recorded because the premise it turns on, that felypressin is the longer-acting agent, is not established by the sources the page cites for it: in dental pulp Olgart 1977 found no felypressin effect at all and Tachibana 2021 found a shallower, faster-recovering fall than with adrenaline. The 1964 study is the one measurement in human skin that supports the premise: felypressin-site pallor persisted unchanged for 3.5 hours or longer, which was the whole observation period, while the adrenaline and noradrenaline sites turned cyanotic centrally within the first hour and kept only a narrow pale rim. The study did not time the anaesthesia, so it cannot say whether pallor outlasted analgesia - only how long the pallor lasted. Recorded on this page as well as on the Lidocaine With Epinephrine Wheals page because the same 1964 study bears on both.
